summary: SBI Life sells life insurance and long-term savings and retirement plans. Customers pay premiums; the company promises a payout on death or at the end of a plan, and invests the premiums in between.
description: Life insurance is a promise. You pay a regular amount, called a premium, and if the insured person dies during the plan, your family receives a lump sum. Other plans work like long-term savings: you pay for years and later receive a set amount, or a regular income in retirement. SBI Life sells such plans to individuals, and to groups such as employees of one employer or borrowers of one lender. Most plans are sold through State Bank of India (SBI) branches, which are the main sales channel, and through agents. Between collecting premiums and paying out, the company invests the money.
money: SBI Life collects premiums and earns returns on the money it invests. From these it pays claims and maturity amounts, commission to the agents and banks that sell its plans, running costs such as staff and technology, and it sets money aside in reserves, which are funds kept to pay future claims. Some plans share their surplus with policyholders as bonuses. Premiums received in a year are not profit, because most of that money is held for future payouts and the rest goes on costs.
customers: Individuals pay premiums to protect their family against their death, or to save for goals such as retirement. Employers pay for group plans that cover their staff, and lenders pay for cover on their borrowers' loans. The person who receives the money when a claim is made is usually the family, not the person who paid.
drivers: Mostly three things: how many new policies it sells, mainly through SBI branches and agents, and whether customers keep paying for years; how its investments perform; and whether claims match the company's assumptions.

groups.title: Protection plans
groups.examples: Cover that pays a lump sum to the family if the insured person dies.
groups.explanation: The customer pays a premium and receives nothing if nothing happens. The cover is for peace of mind about the family's income. Some plans offer lower premiums to non-smokers.

groups.title: Savings plans
groups.examples: Plans that combine cover with guaranteed payouts on some products.
groups.explanation: The customer pays for a set number of years and receives amounts promised in the policy, whatever the markets do. Some plans pay money back in stages.

groups.title: Wealth plans (unit-linked)
groups.examples: Unit-linked insurance plans, often called ULIPs: insurance with money invested in market funds.
groups.explanation: The value of the policy rises and falls with the market value of the fund the customer chose. The customer, not the insurer, carries the investment risk.

groups.title: Retirement and annuity plans
groups.examples: Plans that turn savings into a lifetime income.
groups.explanation: An annuity is a regular payment, usually monthly, for the rest of a person's life. The customer pays in during working years and receives the income after retiring.

groups.title: Group plans
groups.examples: Group term cover, cover on loan borrowers, and plans that help employers fund staff retirement benefits.
groups.explanation: One contract covers many people. A lender, for example, can protect its borrowers so that an outstanding loan is paid if a borrower dies.

basics.title: What is a premium?
basics.text: The payment a customer makes for the insurance, once or regularly. The insurer pools many customers' premiums and uses them to pay the claims of those who need them.

basics.title: What does it mean when a policy lapses?
basics.text: A customer stops paying premiums and the policy ends. Insurers watch this closely, because they spend money to sell a policy and only earn it back if customers keep paying. The share of policies still paid after a period is called persistency.

basics.title: Why do insurers keep large reserves?
basics.text: Money received today is mainly meant for payouts years later. An insurer must keep reserves for future claims, and enough extra capital as a buffer, called the solvency margin.

basics.title: Who regulates insurers?
basics.text: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), which sets rules on products, reserves, selling and investments.

steps.title: A plan is sold
steps.text: A bank branch, an agent or another partner explains a plan and the customer applies. The insurer checks details such as age and health.

steps.title: Premiums come in
steps.text: The customer pays once or regularly. Commission and checking costs on a new policy are mostly paid early.

steps.title: The insurer invests and sets aside reserves
steps.text: Premiums are invested, mostly in bonds, which are loans to governments and companies. Part is put into reserves to pay future claims.

steps.title: Claims and maturities are paid
steps.text: When the insured person dies, or the plan reaches its end, the insurer pays the amount in the policy.

steps.title: Profit is what is left
steps.text: After claims, commissions, running costs and reserves, the surplus is shared with policyholders on some plans, and the rest belongs to shareholders. Cash arrives long before payouts leave.

specifics.title: A bank is both owner and seller
specifics.text: State Bank of India holds more than half of SBI Life, and its branches and rural-bank partners sell most of the new premium. SBI Life is a separate listed company: its premiums, claims and profit are its own, not the bank's.

specifics.title: A very large agent network
specifics.text: Besides the bank, the company lists a large force of individual agents, brokers and other corporate agents. Agents give personal advice, while bank branches bring customers who already trust the bank.

specifics.title: Mostly safe investments
specifics.text: The report says 62.0% of the invested money sits in debt, which means bonds and similar loans, and 93.9% of that debt is government-backed or top-rated. This lowers investment risk for plans where the insurer carries it.

watch: How long do customers keep paying?
Policies earn profit only if premiums keep coming, so frequent lapses make the business less valuable.
Look in the annual report for persistency, the share of policies still paid after 13 months and 61 months, and compare several years.
How much does the business depend on SBI's branches?
One large partner is a strength, but changes in that relationship would change how many policies are sold.
Read the distribution section and compare the share of new business from the bank, agents and other channels over time.
Which kinds of plans are growing?
Protection, savings, wealth and retirement plans earn differently and carry different risks.
Compare the split of new business across plan types in the annual report, year by year, and note which types grow fastest.
How are claims and costs behaving?
If claims or running costs rise faster than premiums, profit shrinks.
Compare benefits paid, commission and operating costs with premiums collected over several years in the financial statements.
How strong is the capital buffer?
Regulators require insurers to hold more capital than their liabilities, so growth needs capital.
Check the solvency margin in the annual report and compare it with the minimum the regulator requires.
risks: Weaker ties with the main bank partner
The report lists distribution risk among its main risks. Because most new premium comes through one bank group, a change in that relationship would slow new business.
A mix of plans that earns less
The report names product mix risk. If customers prefer plans that earn the company less, or guaranteed plans that tie up more capital, profit from each sale falls.

The company names insurance risk, such as more death claims than expected, and investment risk, such as falling markets or defaults on bonds, among its six risk categories. The others are strategy and business, operations, technology and information, and regulation and legal.
Almost all policies are sourced and serviced digitally, and the report lists cybersecurity and data privacy as risks. A breach or outage could hurt customers and reputation.
context: The report describes changes in 2025-26 under the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025. They include raising the limit on foreign ownership of insurers to 100% and extending the free-look period, the time in which a buyer can cancel a new policy without penalty, from 15 to 30 days.
sources: NSE Indices Limited, NIFTY 50 constituent list (SBI Life, symbol SBILIFE)

financialNotes.title: Year ended 31 March 2026: what the audited results show
financialNotes.text: These are standalone figures: SBI Life alone, without any subsidiaries. Total income was ₹111,101 crore. It is mostly premiums, what customers pay for cover (₹99,956 crore after the part passed to other insurers), plus ₹11,062 crore earned by investing money. That part was far lower than last year, mainly, the filing says, because of a drop in the fair value of equity holdings in unit-linked funds, where customers carry the investment risk. Profit after tax was ₹2,470 crore, after a one-time ₹135 crore charge for the new Labour Codes, a labour-law change that raised retirement pay owed to staff for past service.

stepsTitle: From a premium to a payout

quick.title: What it does
quick.text: It sells life insurance, savings and retirement plans to individuals and groups, and invests the premiums it collects.

quick.title: Who pays
quick.text: Individuals pay premiums for protection and savings. Employers and lenders pay for group cover.

quick.title: How it earns
quick.text: Mainly from premiums collected and from returns on investing them. On some plans it keeps a share of the surplus.

quick.title: What it spends on
quick.text: Claims and maturity payouts, commission to banks and agents, staff and technology costs, and money set aside for future claims.

helps.title: A trusted bank sells the plans
helps.text: The company's biggest sales channel is the branch network of its majority owner, which brings many customers who already deal with the bank.

helps.title: Rising interest in protection and retirement
helps.text: The report says household savings are shifting from traditional instruments towards market-linked products. It also describes growing demand for retirement cover as the population ages and more first-time buyers enter.

helps.title: Renewal premiums keep coming
helps.text: Many policies run for years, and existing customers pay renewal premiums each year without a new sale being needed. The report says these renewal premiums depend on customers keeping their policies.

hurts.title: Heavy competition
hurts.text: The report says private life insurers have often grown faster than public ones, so competition for customers is strong and winning them needs spending on distribution.

hurts.title: Selling costs come first
hurts.text: Commission and other selling costs fall when a policy is sold, while the premiums that repay them arrive over many years. The report says that when customers drop policies, the company must spend more to find new ones.

hurts.title: Customers must keep paying
hurts.text: A policy earns its keep only if the customer keeps paying. The report says lower renewal rates reduce premium inflows and long-term profit, and it gives about 85-87% of policies still paid after 13 months and 58-60% after 61 months.
